Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for the Bifactor Indices

Source: R/ci_bifactor_indices.R
ci_bifactor_indices.Rd

Forms nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals for the indices bifactor_indices reports for a fitted bifactor model: the explained common variance (ECV), coefficient omega, omega hierarchical (omega_H) for the general factor, omega hierarchical subscale (omega_HS) for each group factor, the index Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) call coefficient H, the closed form of Hancock and Mueller (2001) applied to one factor's loadings, which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error, and the maximal reliability of each factor under the fitted model, which the index is not (see bifactor_indices). Each replication resamples the cases the fit used, refits the same model with the same estimator, and recomputes every index, so the intervals rest on the same replications (those of the maximal reliability, under improper = "keep", on the proper ones among them). Replications whose solution is improper are set aside by default and counted, and the table says how many.

Usage

ci_bifactor_indices(
  fit,
  general = NULL,
  denominator = c("model_implied", "observed"),
  ci_method = c("percentile", "bca"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  B = 1000L,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1L,
  improper = c("drop", "keep"),
  progress = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_ci_bifactor'
tidy(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_ci_bifactor'
glance(x, ...)

Arguments

fit

A fitted bifactor lavaan model to raw data, as for bifactor_indices: one general factor on all items plus two or more orthogonal group factors, each item on one group factor at most (an item on none is on the general factor alone). A fit that bifactor_indices() refuses is refused here, and so are a multiple-group fit, a fit with a cluster variable or sampling weights, a fit to a covariance matrix, and a fit that did not converge (see Details).

general

Optional name of the general factor, as for bifactor_indices; by default the factor that loads on every item.

denominator

How the total-score variance in the denominators of omega, omega_H, and omega_HS is estimated, as for bifactor_indices: "model_implied" (the default) or "observed". Each replication uses the same setting.

ci_method

The bootstrap interval: "percentile" (the default) or "bca", the bias-corrected and accelerated interval. See Details.

conf_level

Confidence level of the intervals. Defaults to 0.95.

B

Number of bootstrap replications, a single whole number. Defaults to 1000, the package's count for a bootstrap whose every replication refits a model; see Details for the cost. The fewest accepted at the default conf_level is 400 for "percentile" (10 replications beyond each limit; 200 at 0.90, and 2000 at 0.99, which the default does not meet) and 2000 for "bca" (50 beyond each nominal limit), which the default does not meet either: pass B = 2000 or more with ci_method = "bca". A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). The count is held to the number requested: replications set aside afterward are counted and reported in a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped, and an index for which fewer than half of the B replications return a value has its interval withheld (NA) under a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. Where refits can fail, request more than the minimum. See dmar_bootstrap, which also describes options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) for a first look with a smaller B.

seed

Random number seed for the bootstrap. The default NULL uses the current state of the random number generator; a supplied seed is set internally and the caller's state is restored on exit.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the replications are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers (boot's parallel = "multicore") or, on Windows, a socket cluster ("snow"), whose workers load the installed DMAR. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same intervals, counts, and replicates whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set before processx is loaded (see sem_exact_fit_bootstrap).

improper

How a replication whose solution is improper (a standardized loading beyond one or a negative residual variance, a Heywood case) is treated: "drop" (the default) sets it aside, and "keep" uses its indices when every one of them but the maximal reliability, which is not defined for an improper solution, is a proportion. Either way such replications are counted. With "drop" an improper point estimate stops the call. See Details.

progress

NULL (the default), or a function of two arguments that the bootstrap calls as it runs, so that an application can show how far a long bootstrap has gone and let its user stop it (a Shiny app, for example). It is called as progress(done, total), with the number of replications attempted so far and B: after each replication when ncpus = 1, and with more processes after each block of replications they complete together, about a fiftieth of B (ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications, the last block possibly fewer), so that done advances by the block. A BCa interval takes its acceleration from a regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications return a value as there are cases, and from the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, when fewer do or when that regression fails or gives influence values that are not all finite; the jackknife runs at most once in a call, and not at all when no interval is formed or every returned replicate has the same value. While it runs, the callback is called again after each refit (with more processes, after each block of ncpus * ceiling(n / (50 * ncpus)) refits, n the number of cases resampled), with done and total both B, so it can be called more than B times, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished. If the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled, whose elements done and total say how far it got (see dmar_metadata); any other value is ignored. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error, whose message names the callback and which carries done, total, and, as parent, the callback's own condition with its class intact, so that an application can tell a failing callback from a failing analysis. The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same result with or without it, and a callback that draws random numbers leaves the caller's stream as it found it. With NULL nothing is called. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

x

A dmar_ci_bifactor table returned by ci_bifactor_indices().

...

Unused.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_ci_bifactor, dmar_tbl) with one row for each index that applies to a factor, the general factor first (ECV, omega, omega_H, PUC, H, maximal_reliability) and then each group factor (ECV, omega, omega_HS, H, maximal_reliability; its ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items, and its omega the reliability of their total score, as defined under Details of bifactor_indices, which the printed table repeats), and columns factor, index, estimate (the value bifactor_indices() reports, in its table or, for maximal_reliability, in its "maximal_reliability" attribute), se (the standard deviation of the replications used), ci_lower, and ci_upper. PUC has NA in se and the limits, and so does every column of the maximal_reliability rows when the point estimate is improper, and so do the se and limits of any index whose interval is withheld (see require_half under the bootstrap attribute below). The rows depend on the model alone, and the columns never change. Attributes:

bootstrap

The counts and draws: attempted (B), returned (the replications used), failed (those set aside), reasons, error_messages, undetermined (always zero here: it counts the replications that left a polychoric correlation undetermined, which only reliability_omega_categorical meets), improper (improper replications set aside), improper_kept, no_solution (always zero here: it counts the resamples of three items whose correlations admit no single-factor solution, which only the single-factor coefficients of reliability_omega and reliability_H meet), not_converged, too_few_cases (always zero here: it counts the replications the single-factor coefficients set aside for too few distinct cases), improper_rule, caution (TRUE when the replications set aside and the improper ones kept number at least \((1 - C)/2\) of B, with \(C\) the confidence level, so that how they were treated can decide where a limit falls), require_half (TRUE: an index's interval requires at least half of all attempted replications to return a value for it; otherwise its se, ci_lower, and ci_upper are NA, and the warning and the printed line say so; this is an estimability safeguard, not a coverage guarantee), required (the fewest replications a request may ask for, 400 for the percentile interval and 2000 for BCa at the 95 percent level; the count is held to B, not to the replications that return a value) and bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share", the last two when some index has its interval withheld; see dmar_bootstrap), target_returned and target_withheld (for each bootstrapped index, that is, each column of t and named as those columns, the replications that returned a value for it and whether its interval was withheld), acceleration and acceleration_method (one per index), jackknife, ncpus, t (a B by index matrix of the estimates of every replication, one column for each row with an interval, named "factor:index", and NA where a replication gave none; the indices of an improper replication set aside under "drop" are kept here when they are proportions, and its maximal reliabilities are NA), status (the fate of every replication, a factor with levels "proper", "improper", "error", "non_finite", "undetermined", and "not_converged"), and bias (one per column of t, named as its columns: the mean of the replicates the index's interval uses minus its estimate, the bootstrap estimate of its bias; see Details).

B, B_used

The replications requested and the smallest number any reported interval rests on (under improper = "keep", the intervals of the maximal reliability rest on the proper replications, the count of finite values in a maximal reliability column of t, which can be fewer than bootstrap$returned).

n_dropped, B_required, bootstrap_status

B minus B_used, the fewest replications a request may ask for, and the verdict, in the names every bootstrap result of the package carries.

ci_method

The interval of each index, named "factor:index": the method requested, or the percentile label with the reason when a BCa interval could not be formed.

ci_method_requested, conf_level, improper_rule, denominator

The settings of the call.

metric

As for bifactor_indices(): "observed" for continuous items and "latent_response" for ordered items.

general

The name of the general factor.

improper

Whether the point estimate is improper (possible only with improper = "keep").

N, N_incomplete

The rows resampled and how many of them have a missing value.

generics::tidy() returns one row per index with term ("factor:index"), estimate, se, ci_lower, ci_upper, and conf_level; generics::glance() returns one row with the counts and the settings.

Details

Why intervals. The bifactor indices are estimates, and the decisions they are read for (whether a total score is close enough to unidimensional to report alone, whether a subscale carries reliable variance beyond the general factor) are decisions about the population values. A confidence interval says how precisely the sample has located each of them. In the bifactor model of 15 Holzinger and Swineford tests described under Improper replications below, omega_H is 0.577 with a 95 percent interval from 0.468 to 0.672 (B = 1000, seed = 113): 301 cases locate the share of total score variance due to the general factor only to within an interval about 0.2 wide. bifactor_indices() reports the point estimates alone. The intervals are a separate function, rather than an argument of bifactor_indices(), because they need columns that its one-row-per-factor table cannot gain without its shape depending on an argument.

What is resampled. The cases are the rows of data lavaan stored with fit, which are the rows the fit used: under listwise deletion (the default, and lavaan's default for ordered items) the complete rows, and under missing = "ml" (full information maximum likelihood) every row with at least one observed item, each with its own pattern of observed and missing values, so that a resample has the missing data the sample has and each replication is again a full information fit. A row with nothing observed, which lavaan keeps in its stored data but leaves out of the sample, is left out here too, and the number of rows resampled is checked against the number of cases lavaan reports. Rows are drawn with replacement, B times (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993).

How each replication is fit. Each resample is fit with the parameter table and the options of fit: the same model, the same estimator, the same missing data treatment, the same ordered items, and default starting values, as for fit itself. Standard errors and test statistics are not computed in a replication, since no index uses them; robust maximum likelihood (MLR) and WLSMV have the estimates of maximum likelihood and diagonally weighted least squares and differ from them only in those, so a replication is the cheaper fit with the same estimates. Before any resample is drawn, the model is refit this way to the rows of fit itself, and the call stops unless that refit reproduces the point estimates, so the replications are refits of the model the point estimates describe. The indices of each replication are bifactor_indices() of its refit, with the general factor named, so every index is computed as the point estimate is.

Improper replications. A bifactor model is prone to improper solutions, a standardized loading past one or a residual variance below zero, which can come from sampling error around a small residual variance, from a model that does not describe the items, or from a group factor the data barely separate from the general factor, and a resample can give such a solution where the sample does not. A replication is improper when bifactor_indices() flags its solution or lavaan's own check after estimation fails, and the point estimate is judged the same way. For a fit with auxiliary variables (lavaan's aux under full information maximum likelihood) that check is made on the model's own parameters, as sem_fit_measures explains: lavaan's own check also tests the residual covariances of the auxiliary variables, which are not positive definite once one of them is related to the general factor strongly enough, however proper the bifactor solution. A bifactor model of 15 of the Holzinger and Swineford tests (holzinger_swineford: a general factor on all of them, with spatial, verbal, and memory group factors on tests 1–4, 5–9, and 14–19) gave an improper solution in 212 of 1,000 resamples (seed = 113) and did not converge in 17 more. The omega of the improper solutions ranged from 0.84 to 26.5, 132 of them above one; kept, all of them put the upper limit of the 95 percent interval for omega at 13.7 and the lower limit for ECV at 0.004, where the proper replications give [0.855, 0.902] and [0.309, 0.509]. Such values are not sampling variability around a proper structure: a solution in which a residual variance has run away, or in which the general factor has all but vanished (an ECV near zero), is not a perturbation of the sample's solution but a different one, and its indices do not estimate the quantities the point estimate does. The default, improper = "drop", therefore sets them aside. This differs from the default of the reliability family (reliability_omega), where an improper single-factor replication that still yields a coefficient is typically a loading that ran just past one, and keeping it preserves the upper tail of the bootstrap distribution. Setting replications aside conditions the intervals on admissible solutions: they describe the sampling distribution of the indices among resamples that the model fits properly. Yuan and Hayashi (2003, Section 6) argue that a replication that fails because its resample lies far from the model is informative and should be counted rather than discarded; for a test statistic they count it as an extreme value, but an index has no side on which such a replication belongs, so here it is counted and reported rather than placed. Every replication set aside, for any reason, is counted in the bootstrap attribute, named in a warning, and stated under the printed table, and when the replications set aside (or the improper ones kept) reach the tail area of an interval, \((1 - C)/2\) of B for a confidence level \(C\), the warning and the printed line add a caution that the limits depend on how they were treated. When fewer than half of the B replications, or fewer than the number the interval method and the level require (400 for the percentile interval and 2000 for BCa at the 95 percent level; see dmar_bootstrap), return a value for an index, its interval is withheld, and the warning (class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient) and the printed line say so, as in reliability_omega. A run at exactly the required B therefore loses its intervals to a single replication set aside; the default B = 1000 leaves room for them at the 95 percent level. With improper = "keep" an improper replication is used when every index it gives but the maximal reliability, which is not defined for an improper solution (see The maximal reliability below), is a proportion; one whose solution gives an index outside [0, 1] (an omega above one belongs to a composite whose implied error variance is negative) or an H that is not defined (a standardized loading at or past one leaves its item no error variance in H's formula) yields no coefficient and is set aside under either setting, as in the reliability family. So is a replication whose likelihood has no maximum, a residual variance running off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising (see fa_bifactor): it is counted among the replications that raised an error, under a message that names the item, and the run goes on (of the 22 improper replications in 100 of the 15-test model above, seed = 113, 8 were of this kind), while a refit of the data stored with fit that has no maximum stops the call with an error of class dmar_no_maximum. Keeping the admissible indices of improper replications can change their interval limits; the maximal reliability uses only proper replications under either setting. With "drop" an improper point estimate stops the call, since an interval built from proper replications would not describe it; with "keep" it is reported with a warning, unless one of its indices other than the maximal reliability is not defined or lies outside [0, 1]; its maximal reliability, which is not defined, is reported as NA.

The maximal reliability. The rows maximal_reliability give each factor's maximal reliability under the fitted model, \(\lambda_f' R^{-1} \lambda_f\) with \(R\) the item correlations the model reproduces (the "maximal_reliability" attribute of bifactor_indices()): the reliability the optimally weighted items reach as a measure of the factor, and the square of the determinacy of its regression factor score. Like every other index, it is read from bifactor_indices() on each refit, so its interval costs nothing beyond the replications the other indices need. It is a reliability estimate in its own right, as much in need of an interval as omega (Raykov & Penev, 2006, give one for a composite of congeneric measures), and it is the quantity to read beside the index H, which can lie above or below it. It is not defined for an improper solution. With improper = "drop" every replication used is proper, and its intervals rest on the same replications as the others; with "keep" the improper replications kept for the other indices have no maximal reliability, so its intervals rest on the proper replications among them, which are the replications "drop" uses, and the printed table says how many. Its interval is therefore the same under either rule. An improper point estimate, reported under "keep", has no maximal reliability, and these rows then carry no estimate and no interval.

The bias of H and the maximal reliability. The sample H, the closed form the index applies to a factor's loadings, is a positively biased estimator of its population value, and a composite weighted with sample estimates is on average less reliable than the population value: Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, and McIntosh (2019) found both effects pronounced in samples of about 100 and slight beyond about 1,000, for H of a single factor. The maximal reliability is the reliability of weights that are optimal for the sample's estimates and is biased upward in the same way, most of all for a group factor that the data determine weakly. Run with B = 200 in place of its 10, the example below gives a mean of the replicates that exceeds the estimate by 0.031 for the first group factor's maximal reliability (whose replicates have a standard deviation of 0.078) and by 0.019 for its H, against 0.005 for its omega and 0.003 for its omega_HS. The percentile interval takes its limits from the replicates as they fall, and so carries the bias; the BCa interval (ci_method = "bca") moves its limits to correct for the median bias of the replicates. The bias of each index with an interval, the mean of the replicates its interval uses minus the estimate, is the bias element of the bootstrap attribute (PUC, which has no interval, has none, and neither has the maximal reliability of an improper point estimate under improper = "keep"), and the printed table gives it for H and the maximal reliability. Read the maximal reliability as a ceiling that weights estimated from these data will not quite reach.

Other replications set aside. A refit that does not converge is set aside and counted as such, and so is one that raises an error; the warning quotes the most frequent error. For ordered items, a resample that draws no response in some category of an item cannot refit that item's thresholds, and is set aside as an error that says so. The intervals are formed from the replications that remain, and the effective count is the B_used attribute.

The two intervals. The percentile interval takes its limits from the empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates; it respects the [0, 1] range of the indices and is not forced to be symmetric. Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) found it the most consistently accurate of the intervals they compared for the single-factor omega with an observed denominator (their hierarchical omega, which is not the omega_H here), which is the reason it is the default; the sources cited here do not evaluate the coverage of bootstrap intervals for the bifactor indices themselves. The bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) interval moves the two quantile positions to correct for median bias and for the rate at which the variance of the estimator changes with the parameter, which makes it second-order accurate where the percentile interval is first-order accurate (DiCiccio & Efron, 1996). Its acceleration is estimated as boot estimates it, by regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications as cases were used and otherwise, or when that regression fails, by the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, which is run once for all of the indices; an index whose BCa interval cannot be formed gets the percentile interval, with a warning, and the ci_method attribute and the printed line say which. PUC, the proportion of item pairs whose items lie on different group factors, depends only on the model's structure, so it is the same in every replication and has no interval; its row carries the point value with NA limits.

Cost. Each replication is a model fit, so the call costs B fits and, for "bca" with fewer replications used than cases, as many more as there are cases. A proper fit of the 15-test Holzinger and Swineford model takes a few hundredths of a second, but a solution that runs away took seconds before the optimizer stopped, so a model that gives many improper replications is slow to bootstrap as well as hard to interpret. ncpus spreads the replications over several processes, and seed makes a call reproducible. Requires the lavaan and boot packages.

What is refused. A fit that bifactor_indices() refuses (correlated factors, no factor that loads on every item, fewer than two group factors, an item on more than one) is refused, with the same message. So is a multiple-group fit, since resampling the pooled rows would let the group sizes vary from replication to replication (fit each group separately); a fit with a cluster variable, whose cases are not independent and cannot be resampled one at a time; a fit with sampling weights, which a resample of rows does not carry; a fit to a covariance matrix, which has no cases to resample; and a fit that did not converge.

Bootstrap intervals from supplied two-stage fits currently refuse separately stored auxiliary variables: each refit must resample and carry those values with the items. Use an eligible delta interval where available, or explicitly resample and refit them together.

References

Aguirre-Urreta, M. I., Rönkkö, M., & McIntosh, C. N. (2019). A cautionary note on the finite sample behavior of maximal reliability. Psychological Methods, 24(2), 236–252. doi:10.1037/met0000176

DiCiccio, T. J., & Efron, B. (1996). Bootstrap confidence intervals. Statistical Science, 11(3), 189–228.

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Hancock, G. R., & Mueller, R. O. (2001). Rethinking construct reliability within latent variable systems. In R. Cudeck, S. du Toit, & D. Sörbom (Eds.), Structural equation modeling: Present and future (pp. 195–216). Scientific Software International.

Kelley, K., & Pornprasertmanit, S. (2016). Confidence intervals for population reliability coefficients: Evaluation of methods, recommendations, and software for composite measures. Psychological Methods, 21(1), 69–92. doi:10.1037/a0040086

Raykov, T., & Penev, S. (2006). A direct method for obtaining approximate standard error and confidence interval of maximal reliability for composites with congeneric measures. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 41(1), 15–28. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr4101_2

Reise, S. P. (2012). The rediscovery of bifactor measurement models. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 47(5), 667–696. doi:10.1080/00273171.2012.715555

Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: Calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137–150. doi:10.1037/met0000045

Yuan, K.-H., & Hayashi, K. (2003). Bootstrap approach to inference and power analysis based on three test statistics for covariance structure models. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 56, 93–110.

Examples

# The nine-item bifactor model of ?bifactor_indices: one general factor
# and three orthogonal group factors, simulated so that resamples give
# proper solutions and the example runs quickly. (The 15-test
# Holzinger and Swineford model of Details gives an improper solution
# in a fifth of its resamples, each of which took seconds to fit.)
set.seed(113)
n <- 600
g <- rnorm(n); grp <- list(rnorm(n), rnorm(n), rnorm(n))
X <- vapply(1:9, function(i)
  0.5 * g + 0.5 * grp[[ceiling(i / 3)]] + sqrt(0.5) * rnorm(n), numeric(n))
colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:9)
model <- "g  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
          f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
          f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
          f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9"
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, data = as.data.frame(X),
                   orthogonal = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE)

# Every replication refits the bifactor model. B = 10 keeps the
# example quick and is below the 400 a reported interval needs; the
# option lets it run and the warning says so. A reported interval
# deserves the default B = 1000. A resample whose solution is improper
# is set aside, and the warning and the printed lines count it.
old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)
ci <- ci_bifactor_indices(fit, B = 10, seed = 113)
#> Warning: ci_bifactor_indices(): B = 10 is below the 400 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 10 replications each limit rests on about 0.3 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 400. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result.
options(old)
ci
#>  factor index               estimate se    ci_lower ci_upper
#>  g      ECV                 0.547    0.044 0.484    0.637

#>  g      PUC                 0.750    <NA>  <NA>     <NA>    
#>  g      H                   0.769    0.019 0.747    0.814   
#>  g      maximal_reliability 0.678    0.030 0.647    0.752   
#>  f1     ECV                 0.609    0.085 0.487    0.813   
#>  f1     omega               0.727    0.017 0.707    0.760   
#>  f1     omega_HS            0.280    0.058 0.135    0.362   
#>  f1     H                   0.412    0.083 0.226    0.516   
#>  f1     maximal_reliability 0.396    0.089 0.220    0.537   
#>  f2     ECV                 0.543    0.077 0.456    0.708   
#>  f2     omega               0.756    0.017 0.736    0.787   
#>  f2     omega_HS            0.345    0.057 0.226    0.424   
#>  f2     H                   0.477    0.055 0.362    0.557   
#>  f2     maximal_reliability 0.456    0.057 0.335    0.545   
#>  f3     ECV                 0.490    0.079 0.425    0.646   
#>  f3     omega               0.743    0.017 0.707    0.761   
#>  f3     omega_HS            0.377    0.059 0.257    0.428   
#>  f3     H                   0.506    0.058 0.377    0.558   
#>  f3     maximal_reliability 0.494    0.064 0.358    0.556

#> Intervals: percentile bootstrap over the 600 rows the fit used, with improper replications set aside; PUC depends only on which items share a group factor, so it has no interval
#> 
#> Bootstrap estimates of bias (mean of the replicates used minus the estimate): H g 0.00261, f1 0.0272, f2 0.014, f3 -0.0198; maximal_reliability g 0.00693, f1 0.0441, f2 0.0185, f3 -0.0185
#> 
#> For a group factor, ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items (one minus it is the group factor's share), and omega is the reliability of their total score
#> H is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error; maximal_reliability is the reliability the optimally weighted items reach as a measure of the factor under the fitted model
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 10 replications attempted, 10 returned a value; at least 400 are required for a reported interval. Exploratory: below the number required for a reported interval

# Every replication's indices, and what happened to it.
head(attr(ci, "bootstrap")$t[, c("g:omega", "g:omega_H", "g:H",
                                 "g:maximal_reliability")])
